_comment: One story is an ordered list of pages. Each page is one illustration and one spoken line; the owl turns the page when the line finishes. A page's `audio` is a filename in audio/ — when it is absent or the file is missing, the owl speaks the text with the synthesiser instead, so a half-recorded pack still plays.
_length: The brief asks for 60 to 120 seconds per story. At a slow bedtime reading of about 130 words a minute that is 130 to 260 words; a test asserts every story lands in that band.
_gap: The brief asks for at least six stories per hero. One per hero is here, enough to build and test Stories mode. The rest is writing, not engineering.

pages.text: One frosty morning, when the whole wood was quiet and white, Fern the Fox found a little red mitten lying in the snow.
She turned it over with her nose. It was soft, and warm, and much too small for her paw.
Somebody with very small hands, thought Fern, must be very cold indeed.
So she picked it up carefully in her teeth and set off along the path, past the frozen stream and the old stone wall.
She asked the rabbits under the hedge. They wriggled their noses and said they had never worn a mitten in their lives.
She asked the sleepy owl in the oak tree. He opened one eye, thought for a long moment, and said, try the little house under the roots.
Fern went down the slope, under the roots, to a round door no taller than her ear.
Inside sat a small brown mouse with one paw tucked under her chin, trying very hard not to mind the cold.
Fern set the mitten down on the doorstep. The mouse looked at it, and then at Fern, and her whiskers went quite still.
Then she put it on, and smiled, and the whole wood felt a little warmer than before.
Pip the Bunny was the smallest bunny in the whole meadow, and the meadow was very large.
In summer the grass grew so tall that Pip could never see where he was going.
His brothers could see the pond. His sisters could see the hill. Pip could only see grass.
He tried jumping, again and again, until his legs were tired and the sky had turned gold.
He tried standing on a smooth grey stone. He still could not see over the top.
So Pip sat down in the middle of all that grass, and stopped trying to see over it.
And down there, close to the ground, he found a beetle in a shining green coat.
He found clover, sweeter than anything up high, and a snail carrying his house very slowly home.
Best of all, he found a narrow winding path that only somebody very small could ever fit through.
Being small, Pip decided as he followed it home, was not so bad after all.
Bramble the Bear loved honey more than anything else in the world.
He loved it more than raspberries, more than sleeping, and very nearly more than his own mother.
One afternoon he found a round jar of it standing on a high wooden shelf.
He reached up on his toes, took it down with both paws, and tipped it carefully over.
But honey does not hurry. Honey has never hurried for anybody.
It slid down the side of the jar slower than a snail on a cold morning.
Bramble huffed. Bramble sighed. Bramble shook the jar, which did not help at all.
At last he sat down on the floor with the jar in his lap, and simply waited.
And while he waited he watched the afternoon sun come through the window, and the dust turning slowly in it.
When the honey finally reached his paw, it was the sweetest thing he had ever tasted.
Tilly the Mouse lived behind the kitchen wall, in a nest of wool and paper.
She liked almost everything about her house, except for one thing.
She did not like the dark corner behind the cupboard, where the light never reached.
Every night she ran past it very fast, with her eyes shut tight and her heart going quickly.
One night, as she hurried by, she heard a sound from the corner. A very small sound.
Tilly stopped. She stood quite still in the middle of the floor and listened.
The sound came again, smaller than before, and rather sad.
So Tilly took one step closer. Then another. Then, slowly, she opened her eyes.
It was only a beetle, quite lost, turning in circles and looking for the way home.
Tilly showed him the crack under the door. And after that night, the corner was only ever a corner.
Nub the Hedgehog lived under the garden hedge, in a heap of dry brown leaves.
He liked the leaves. He liked the quiet. He was not at all sure about anybody else.
Whenever somebody came near, Nub rolled himself into a tight round ball.
He would stay that way, very small and very prickly, until whoever it was went away again.
And they always did go away, because nobody likes waiting for a ball of spines.
But one warm evening a small voice said hello, and then it did something new.
It sat down in the leaves beside him, and it waited.
It waited while the sun went down. It waited while the first star came out.
So Nub uncurled, just a very little, and looked out with one careful eye.
And there was a friend, sitting quietly in the leaves, who had been there the whole time.
